The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume AC and Countable Choice, the finite-dimensional linear contextual bandit model, and LinUCB with $\beta_t=\max\{1,\rho_t^2\}$ as defined in the algorithm. Let $\delta\in(0,1)$ be the confidence input to LinUCB. Suppose also that for every round $t$,

$$\sup_{a,b\in\mathcal A_t}\langle\theta^*,a-b\rangle\le1.$$

Define the random pseudo-regret by

$$\widehat R_n:=\sum_{t=1}^n\left(\max_{a\in\mathcal A_t}\langle\theta^*,a\rangle-\langle\theta^*,A_t\rangle\right).$$

Then, with probability at least $1-\delta$,

$$\widehat R_n\le\sqrt{8n\beta_n\log\!\left(\frac{\det V_n}{\det V_0}\right)}\le\sqrt{8dn\beta_n\log\!\left(1+\frac{nL^2}{d\lambda}\right)}.$$

**Algorithm properties.** For every admissible model input, the algorithm also completes exactly $n$ rounds and outputs $(A_t,X_t)_{t=1}^n$ and $(V_n,b_n,\widehat\theta_n)$. Count exact real arithmetic operations, comparisons, square roots, and logarithms with unit cost, and exclude generation of contexts, features, and rewards. Let $F$ be the rounds with finite action sets and let $m_t$ be the number of available actions at round $t\in F$; let $K$ be the compact-feature rounds. The procedure makes exactly $|K|$ calls to the supplied maximizing selector and uses $O(nd^3+d^2\sum_{t\in F}m_t)$ operations apart from selector costs.

**Inputs and admissibility.** Take the finite-dimensional linear contextual bandit model and a confidence level $\delta\in(0,1)$. At each round, the nonempty available action set is finite and ordered with its feature vectors, or the available feature set is compact with a supplied attained measurable predictable maximizer for the score below. In the finite case evaluate the score for each action's feature and resolve ties by the first action. All model assumptions, including $\lambda>0$, the feature and parameter bounds, pre-reward information, and the conditional noise bound, are in force.

**Outputs.** Before each reward is observed, output the selected feature $A_t$; after the reward $X_t$ is observed, record it. At the horizon return the online sequence $(A_t,X_t)_{t=1}^n$ and terminal state $(V_n,b_n,\widehat\theta_n)$.

Initialize $V_0=\lambda I_d$, $b_0=0$, $\widehat\theta_0=0$, $W_0=\lambda^{-1}I_d$, and $D_0=\lambda^d$. At each round $t=1,\ldots,n$, compute

$$\rho_t=\sqrt\lambda\,m_2+\sqrt{2\log(1/\delta)+\log(D_{t-1}/D_0)},\qquad \beta_t=\max\{1,\rho_t^2\},$$

Next select an available feature vector

$$A_t\in\arg\max_{a\in\mathcal A_t}\left\{\langle\widehat\theta_{t-1},a\rangle+\sqrt{\beta_t}\,\sqrt{a^{\mathsf T}W_{t-1}a}\right\}.$$

For a finite ordered action set, evaluate every action's score and take the first maximizing action's feature; for a compact feature set, call the supplied selector once. After observing reward $X_t$, update

$$V_t=V_{t-1}+A_tA_t^{\mathsf T},\qquad b_t=b_{t-1}+A_tX_t.$$

Then compute the updated matrix state $W_t,D_t$ from $V_t$ by the following exact row procedure. Form the augmented matrix $M=[V_t\mid I_d]$, set $s=1$ and $D=1$, and for $k=0,\ldots,d-1$ choose the least row index $i\ge k$ whose current left-block entry $M_{ik}$ is nonzero. If no such row exists, return failure. If $i\ne k$, swap rows $i$ and $k$ and replace $s$ by $-s$. Set $p_k=M_{kk}$, replace $D$ by $Dp_k$, divide row $k$ by $p_k$, and for every $j\ne k$ set $\operatorname{row}_j\leftarrow\operatorname{row}_j-M_{jk}\operatorname{row}_k$. After the loop set $W_t$ to the right block and $D_t=sD$, and set $\widehat\theta_t=W_tb_t$. For a compact feature set the supplied selector must return an attained maximizing feature measurably from pre-reward information.

Let $d,n\ge1$, let $\lambda>0$, let $L\ge0$, and let $a_1,\ldots,a_n\in\mathbb R^d$ satisfy $\|a_t\|_2\le L$. Put $V_t=\lambda I_d+\sum_{s=1}^t a_sa_s^{\mathsf T}$ and $V_0=\lambda I_d$, and define $\operatorname{tr}(M)=\sum_{i=1}^d M_{ii}$. Then

$$0<\det V_t\quad(0\le t\le n),\qquad \log\!\left(\frac{\det V_n}{\det V_0}\right)\le d\log\!\left(1+\frac{nL^2}{d\lambda}\right).$$

Fix integers $d,n\ge1$, real parameters $\lambda>0$, $L\ge1$, and $m_2\ge0$, and a deterministic vector $\theta^*\in\mathbb R^d$ with $\|\theta^*\|_2\le m_2$. Replacing any finite feature bound by its maximum with $1$ makes the convention $L\ge1$ harmless. Work on a probability space with a filtration $(\mathcal F_t)_{t=0}^{n+1}$ satisfying $\mathcal F_t\subseteq\mathcal F_{t+1}$.

At round $t$, before reward noise is observed, the history sigma-algebra $\mathcal F_t$ contains all contexts, choices, and feedback through rounds $s<t$, as well as the current context $C_t$, the nonempty available action set, and its available feature set $\mathcal A_t\subseteq\mathbb R^d$. The features arise from a measurable map $\psi_t$ between spaces with declared measurable structures by $a=\psi_t(C_t,\bar a)$ for available actions $\bar a$. The feature set is finite or compact in the Euclidean topology, every candidate $a\in\mathcal A_t$ satisfies $\|a\|_2\le L$, and the selected feature $A_t=\psi_t(C_t,a_t)\in\mathcal A_t$ is $\mathcal F_t$-measurable. The true-mean maximum is attained and its value is $\mathcal F_t$-measurable. A policy using LinUCB must also select an attained upper-confidence maximizer measurably from the pre-reward information; finite ordered action sets select the first maximizer, while a compact set is used only when such a predictable selection is supplied.

After $A_t$ is selected, the reward $X_t$ is observed, where $\eta_t$ is an $\mathcal F_{t+1}$-measurable real random variable and

$$X_t=\langle\theta^*,A_t\rangle+\eta_t.$$

For every $q\in\mathbb R$, require $e^{q\eta_t}$ to be integrable and its conditional expectation version to satisfy

$$\mathbb E[e^{q\eta_t}\mid\mathcal F_t]\le e^{q^2/2}\quad\text{almost surely}.$$

This is conditional $1$-sub-Gaussian noise with the pre-reward convention for $\mathcal F_t$. No independence between rounds is assumed. For $0\le t\le n$, define the unaveraged ridge information matrix and response sum by

$$V_t:=\lambda I_d+\sum_{s=1}^t A_sA_s^{\mathsf T},\qquad b_t:=\sum_{s=1}^t A_sX_s,$$

with empty sums equal to $0$. Set $\widehat\theta_0=0$ and $\widehat\theta_t=V_t^{-1}b_t$ for $t\ge1$. For a real symmetric matrix $M$ satisfying $v^{\mathsf T}Mv>0$ for all nonzero $v$, write $\|v\|_M:=\sqrt{v^{\mathsf T}Mv}$. The estimate $\widehat\theta_t$ is the unique minimizer of $\sum_{s=1}^t(X_s-\langle\theta,A_s\rangle)^2+\lambda\|\theta\|_2^2$; the sum is not divided by $t$.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

- If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, its **expectation** is the
  extended-valued integral
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P\in[0,+\infty].$$
- If $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ or $X:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is integrable in the sense
  of [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], its
  **expectation** is again
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P,$$
  now a finite real or complex number.

For an integrable real random variable,
$$\mathbb E[X]=\mathbb E[X^+]-\mathbb E[X^-],$$
where $X^+$ and $X^-$ are its positive and negative parts.

Let $X,Y$ be integrable real or complex random variables on one probability
space.

1. For scalars $a,b$,
   $$\mathbb E[aX+bY]=a\,\mathbb E[X]+b\,\mathbb E[Y].$$
2. If $X$ and $Y$ are real-valued and $X\le Y$ almost surely, then
   $$\mathbb E[X]\le\mathbb E[Y].$$
3. $$|\mathbb E[X]|\le\mathbb E[|X|].$$

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space and let $A\in\mathcal F$.
Then the indicator $\mathbf 1_A$ satisfies
$$\mathbb E[\mathbf 1_A]=\mathbb P(A).$$

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

In the finite-dimensional linear contextual bandit model, put

$$G_t:=\sum_{s=1}^t A_sA_s^{\mathsf T},\qquad S_t:=\sum_{s=1}^t A_s\eta_s\qquad(0\le t\le n).$$

Give each finite real matrix space its entrywise Euclidean topology and corresponding Borel sigma-algebra. Then $V_t$, $b_t$, $G_t$, $S_t$, and $D_t:=\det(V_t)$ are $\mathcal F_{t+1}$-measurable matrix, vector, or real random elements, and the ridge estimate $\widehat\theta_t=V_t^{-1}b_t$ is an $\mathcal F_{t+1}$-measurable $\mathbb R^d$-valued random element for every $0\le t\le n$.

**Inputs and admissibility.** Take the finite-dimensional linear contextual bandit model and a confidence level $\delta\in(0,1)$. At each round, the nonempty available action set is finite and ordered with its feature vectors, or the available feature set is compact with a supplied attained measurable predictable maximizer for the score below. In the finite case evaluate the score for each action's feature and resolve ties by the first action. All model assumptions, including $\lambda>0$, the feature and parameter bounds, pre-reward information, and the conditional noise bound, are in force.

**Outputs.** Before each reward is observed, output the selected feature $A_t$; after the reward $X_t$ is observed, record it. At the horizon return the online sequence $(A_t,X_t)_{t=1}^n$ and terminal state $(V_n,b_n,\widehat\theta_n)$.

Initialize $V_0=\lambda I_d$, $b_0=0$, $\widehat\theta_0=0$, $W_0=\lambda^{-1}I_d$, and $D_0=\lambda^d$. At each round $t=1,\ldots,n$, compute

$$\rho_t=\sqrt\lambda\,m_2+\sqrt{2\log(1/\delta)+\log(D_{t-1}/D_0)},\qquad \beta_t=\max\{1,\rho_t^2\},$$

Next select an available feature vector

$$A_t\in\arg\max_{a\in\mathcal A_t}\left\{\langle\widehat\theta_{t-1},a\rangle+\sqrt{\beta_t}\,\sqrt{a^{\mathsf T}W_{t-1}a}\right\}.$$

For a finite ordered action set, evaluate every action's score and take the first maximizing action's feature; for a compact feature set, call the supplied selector once. After observing reward $X_t$, update

$$V_t=V_{t-1}+A_tA_t^{\mathsf T},\qquad b_t=b_{t-1}+A_tX_t.$$

Then compute the updated matrix state $W_t,D_t$ from $V_t$ by the following exact row procedure. Form the augmented matrix $M=[V_t\mid I_d]$, set $s=1$ and $D=1$, and for $k=0,\ldots,d-1$ choose the least row index $i\ge k$ whose current left-block entry $M_{ik}$ is nonzero. If no such row exists, return failure. If $i\ne k$, swap rows $i$ and $k$ and replace $s$ by $-s$. After the loop set $W_t$ to the right block and $D_t=sD$, and set $\widehat\theta_t=W_tb_t$. derivations.claim: With $\delta=1/n$, [F2] and [F3] give $$\beta_n\le1+\left(\sqrt\lambda m_2+\sqrt{2\log n+dq_n}\right)^2\le1+2\lambda m_2^2+4\log n+2dq_n.$$ The first inequality uses $\max\{1,x\}\le1+x$ for $x\ge0$; the second uses $(a+b)^2\le2a^2+2b^2$.

Since $nL\ge2$, $\log n\le\log(nL)$ and $$1+\frac{nL^2}{d\lambda}\le1+\frac{nL^2}{\lambda}\le nL\left(1+\frac{L}{\lambda}\right).$$ By [F6], $q_n\le\log(nL)+\log(1+L/\lambda)\le c\log(nL)$. Hence step 1.1 and $d\ge1$, $\log(nL)\ge\log2$ imply $\beta_n\le C_1d\log(nL)$.
Step 2.1 and the definition of $B_n$ give $$B_n=\sqrt{8dn\beta_nq_n}\le\sqrt{8C_1c}\,d\sqrt n\log(nL)$$ pointwise. By [F7], $B_n$ is measurable; this deterministic bound makes it integrable.

By [F1] with $\delta=1/n$, there is a measurable event $E$ with $\mathbb P(E)\ge1-1/n$ on which $\widehat R_n\le B_n$. By [F4], $0\le\widehat R_n\le n$ on every outcome. Therefore $\widehat R_n\le B_n\mathbf1_E+n\mathbf1_{E^c}$ pointwise. Taking expectations and using [F5], [F7], and step 2.1 gives $$R_n\le\mathbb E[B_n\mathbf1_E]+n\mathbb P(E^c)\le\mathbb E[B_n]+1.$$

Let $U$ be a nonempty set of possible records and let $\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$. A database is a function $D:U\to\mathbb N_0$ with finite support $\operatorname{supp}(D)=\{u\in U:D(u)\ne0\}$; $D(u)$ is the number of occurrences of record $u$. Let $\mathcal D$ be the set of databases and equip it with the power-set sigma-algebra. For $u\in U$, let $\mathbf 1_{\{u\}}$ be the function that is one at $u$ and zero elsewhere. Two databases $D,D'\in\mathcal D$ are neighbors, written $D\sim D'$, when $D'=D+\mathbf 1_{\{u\}}$ or $D=D'+\mathbf 1_{\{u\}}$ for some $u\in U$.

A randomized mechanism with output measurable space $(Y,\mathcal B)$ is a probability kernel $K$ from $\mathcal D$ to $Y$: for each $D\in\mathcal D$, $A\mapsto K(D,A)$ is a probability measure on $(Y,\mathcal B)$, and for each $A\in\mathcal B$, $D\mapsto K(D,A)$ is measurable. Given $\varepsilon\ge0$ and $0\le\delta\le1$, the mechanism is $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-differentially private if, for every ordered neighboring pair $D\sim D'$ and every output event $A\in\mathcal B$,

$$
K(D,A)\le e^{\varepsilon}K(D',A)+\delta.
$$

The mechanism is $\varepsilon$-differentially private, or pure $\varepsilon$-differentially private, when $\delta=0$. The ordered-pair quantifier includes both directions because $\sim$ is symmetric.

A **measurable space** is a pair $(X,\mathcal A)$ consisting of a set $X$ and a
sigma-algebra $\mathcal A$ on $X$ ([[def-sigma-algebra]]). The members of
$\mathcal A$ are the **measurable subsets** of $X$.

A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ ([[def-measure]]). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** ([[def-measure-space]]); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in [[def-measure]] and [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

Let $k>1$ and $n\ge1$ be integers, and let $\eta>0$. Use the finite-arm bandit protocol with rewards in $[0,1]$ and conditional sampling as specified in the bandit importance-weighted estimator definition. Initialize $\widehat S_{0,i}=0$ for each $i\in[k]$. For rounds $t=1,\ldots,n$, perform the following operations:

1. Set
   $$
   P_{t,i}=\frac{\exp(\eta\widehat S_{t-1,i})}{\sum_{j=1}^k\exp(\eta\widehat S_{t-1,j})},\qquad i\in[k].
   $$
2. Draw a measurable finite-valued action $A_t$ with conditional probabilities $\mathbb P(A_t=i\mid\mathcal F_{t-1})=P_{t,i}$, and observe only $X_t=x_{t,A_t}$.
3. Form the loss estimates $\widehat Y_{t,i}=\mathbf1\{A_t=i\}(1-X_t)/P_{t,i}$ and reward estimates $\widehat X_{t,i}=1-\widehat Y_{t,i}$ for every $i\in[k]$.
4. Update $\widehat S_{t,i}=\widehat S_{t-1,i}+\widehat X_{t,i}$ for every $i\in[k]$.

The output is $(P_t,A_t,X_t,\widehat X_t,\widehat Y_t)_{t=1}^n$ and $\widehat S_n$. These operations use exact real arithmetic. The procedure assumes a probability space carrying the stated measurable draws; it makes no probability-space construction claim. Normalizing the weights $\exp(\eta\widehat S_{t-1,i})$ is the exponential-weights step used by Hedge.

Let $N,T\ge1$ be integers, let $[N]=\{1,\ldots,N\}$ be the expert set, and let $\epsilon>0$. At each round $t=1,\ldots,T$, a finite loss vector $\ell_t=(\ell_t(1),\ldots,\ell_t(N))\in[0,\infty)^N$ is revealed after the learner's choice. Initialize $W_1(i)=1$ for every $i\in[N]$. At round $t$, set
$$x_t(i):=\frac{W_t(i)}{\sum_{j=1}^{N}W_t(j)},\qquad i\in[N],$$
Let $\mathcal H_{t-1}$ be the pre-round history sigma-algebra generated by the previously played choices and all previously revealed loss vectors (any random loss vector is assumed measurable on the protocol's probability space). The weights and $x_t$ are $\mathcal H_{t-1}$-measurable. Draw a measurable expert choice $I_t\in[N]$ with conditional distribution
$$\mathbb P(I_t=i\mid\mathcal H_{t-1})=x_t(i)\quad\text{almost surely},\qquad i\in[N],$$
and play $I_t$. After observing the whole vector $\ell_t$, update
$$W_{t+1}(i):=W_t(i)\exp(-\epsilon\ell_t(i)),\qquad i\in[N].$$
The output is the distributions $x_1,\ldots,x_T$, the sampled choices $I_1,\ldots,I_T$, and the final weights. The protocol assumes a probability space carrying the stated measurable draws; no probability-space construction is claimed.

Let $k,n\ge1$ be integers, let $[k]=\{1,\ldots,k\}$, and let
$$
\Delta_k=\left\{p\in[0,1]^k:\sum_{i=1}^k p_i=1\right\}.
$$
On a probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$, let $(\mathcal F_t)_{t=0}^n$ be the discrete filtration generated by the complete histories through round $t$, with $\mathcal F_0$ trivial; a complete pre-action history records past reward vectors, actions, and observed rewards. A reward vector is either fixed in advance or a deterministic function of the complete pre-action history. Thus, at a finite horizon with finitely many arms, there are finitely many possible histories. Before action $A_t$ is drawn, the current reward vector $x_t=(x_{t,1},\ldots,x_{t,k})\in[0,1]^k$ and sampling distribution $P_t=(P_{t,1},\ldots,P_{t,k})\in\Delta_k$ are $\mathcal F_{t-1}$-measurable, and $P_{t,i}>0$ for every $i$. The finite-valued measurable action $A_t\in[k]$ has conditional law $\mathbb P(A_t=i\mid\mathcal F_{t-1})=P_{t,i}$. The learner observes only $X_t=x_{t,A_t}$ and sets
$$
Y_t=1-X_t,\qquad y_{t,i}=1-x_{t,i},\qquad \widehat Y_{t,i}=\frac{\mathbf 1\{A_t=i\}Y_t}{P_{t,i}},\qquad \widehat X_{t,i}=1-\widehat Y_{t,i}.
$$
The quantity $\widehat Y_{t,i}$ is the importance-weighted loss estimate for arm $i$, and $\widehat X_{t,i}$ is its corresponding reward estimate. A fixed reward sequence is the oblivious case; allowing $x_t$ to depend on the history available before $A_t$ is drawn gives the non-anticipating past-adaptive case. In either case the current reward vector is chosen before the current action. For finite horizons and finite action histories generated by such a fixed or deterministic history-dependent sequence, all these estimates are finite and integrable.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].

This is a real power series centred at $0$ ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.

For every real $x$, $\exp(x)>0$ and
$$\exp(-x)=\frac1{\exp(x)}.$$
The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.

routine_steps.claim: Since $\widehat S_{0,1}=\widehat S_{0,2}=0$, Exp3 starts with probabilities $(1/2,1/2)$. If $A_1=1$, then $Y_1=0$ and $\widehat X_{1,1}=\widehat X_{1,2}=1$, so the next Exp3 distribution is uniform. If $A_1=2$, then $Y_1=1$, $P_{1,2}=1/2$, and $(\widehat Y_{1,1},\widehat Y_{1,2})=(0,2)$; hence $\widehat X_1=(1,-1)$ and the next distribution is $(\exp(\eta)/(\exp(\eta)+\exp(-\eta)),\exp(-\eta)/(\exp(\eta)+\exp(-\eta)))$.
Full-information Hedge uses $\epsilon=\eta$ and sees losses $(0,1)$, so its next weights are $(1,\exp(-\eta))$ and its normalized distribution is $(\exp(\eta)/(\exp(\eta)+1),1/(\exp(\eta)+1))$.

By [F4] and [F6], $\exp(\eta)>1$, so Hedge's first probability exceeds $1/2$ and differs from Exp3's first probability after $A_1=1$. Also $\exp(2\eta)>\exp(\eta)$, so the odds ratio after $A_1=2$ is $\exp(2\eta)$ for Exp3 and $\exp(\eta)$ for Hedge; these distributions differ as well.

Let $S$ be a finite set, possibly empty, let $\mathcal R$ be a finite subset of $\mathbb R$, and for each $s\in S$ let $A(s)$ be a finite nonempty set. Here **finite** means bijective with a natural number, and the **discrete sigma-algebra** on a set is its power set. Write $D=\{(s,a):s\in S,\ a\in A(s)\}$. A **finite Markov decision process (MDP)** consists of these sets and numbers $p(s',\rho\mid s,a)\in[0,1]$, indexed by $(s,a)\in D$, $s'\in S$, and $\rho\in\mathcal R$, with

$$ \sum_{s'\in S}\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal R}p(s',\rho\mid s,a)=1 \qquad ((s,a)\in D). $$

Equip each set used here, including $D$, with its power-set (discrete) sigma-algebra. Thus $p$ is the point-mass form of a probability kernel from $D$ to $S\times\mathcal R$: each input assigns a probability measure on $S\times\mathcal R$, and every event section is measurable. The joint law allows the next state and reward to be dependent. Define the expected reward and state-transition probabilities by

$$ r(s,a)=\sum_{s'\in S}\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal R}\rho\,p(s',\rho\mid s,a), \qquad P(s'\mid s,a)=\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal R}p(s',\rho\mid s,a). $$

If $\mathcal R\ne\emptyset$, put $M=\max_{\rho\in\mathcal R}|\rho|$; if $\mathcal R=\emptyset$, put $M=0$. A stationary Markov policy is a family of probabilities $\pi(a\mid s)\ge0$ with $\sum_{a\in A(s)}\pi(a\mid s)=1$ for every $s\in S$. A deterministic policy is a function $\pi$ with $\pi(s)\in A(s)$ for every $s$. When $S=\emptyset$, these families and policies are the unique empty functions and all statewise formulas are vacuous.

For a finite MDP, a discount $0\le\gamma<1$, and a stationary Markov policy $\pi$, define the **policy Bellman operator** $T^\pi:\mathbb R^S\to\mathbb R^S$ by

$$ (T^\pi V)(s)=\sum_{a\in A(s)}\pi(a\mid s)\left[r(s,a)+\gamma\sum_{s'\in S}P(s'\mid s,a)V(s')\right]\qquad(s\in S). $$

If $S=\emptyset$, this is the unique map from $\mathbb R^S$ to itself.

For a finite MDP and a discount $0\le\gamma<1$, define the **Bellman optimality operator** $T^*:\mathbb R^S\to\mathbb R^S$ by

$$ (T^*V)(s)=\max_{a\in A(s)}\left[r(s,a)+\gamma\sum_{s'\in S}P(s'\mid s,a)V(s')\right]\qquad(s\in S). $$

The maximum exists because each $A(s)$ is finite and nonempty. If $S=\emptyset$, this is the unique map from $\mathbb R^S$ to itself.

Let a finite MDP and a discount $0\le\gamma<1$ be fixed. For $U\in\mathbb R^S$, define $\|U\|_\infty=0$ if $S=\emptyset$, and $\|U\|_\infty=\max_{s\in S}|U(s)|$ otherwise. For every stationary policy $\pi$ and all $V,W\in\mathbb R^S$,

$$ \|T^\pi V-T^\pi W\|_\infty\le\gamma\|V-W\|_\infty. $$

The Bellman optimality operator satisfies the same inequality. Each of $T^\pi$ and $T^*$ has exactly one fixed point in $\mathbb R^S$. The contraction constant is the nonnegative number $\gamma$.

derivations.claim: Under the point-mass stationary policy choosing $a$, [F1] and [F2] give $T^a(v)=1+\tfrac12v$, whose fixed point solves $v=1+\tfrac12v$, hence is $v=2$. Under the point-mass stationary policy choosing $b$, the equation is $v=3+\tfrac12v$, hence its unique fixed point is $v=6$.

For a stationary policy with $\pi(b\mid s)=\theta$, the expected one-step reward is $(1-\theta)\cdot1+\theta\cdot3=1+2\theta$, so $T^\pi(v)=1+2\theta+\tfrac12v$ and its unique fixed point is $v=2+4\theta$.

Adding $2$ to each reward changes the deterministic maps to $T^{a,+}(v)=3+\tfrac12v$ and $T^{b,+}(v)=5+\tfrac12v$, whose fixed points are $6$ and $10$. For the stochastic policy, the expected one-step reward becomes $3+2\theta$, so $T^{\pi,+}(v)=3+2\theta+\tfrac12v$ and the unique fixed point is $6+4\theta$. All these policy values increase by $4$, and the difference between the deterministic values remains $4$.

At $v=6$, the original action values are $1+\tfrac12\cdot6=4$ and $3+\tfrac12\cdot6=6$, so $T^*6=6$ and $b$ is greedy; [F3] makes $6$ the unique optimal fixed point. After the shift, at $v=10$ the action values are $3+\tfrac12\cdot10=8$ and $5+\tfrac12\cdot10=10$, so the shifted optimality operator fixes $10$ and $b$ is greedy there; [F3] again gives uniqueness.

Let $U$ be a nonempty set of possible records and let $\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$. A database is a function $D:U\to\mathbb N_0$ with finite support $\operatorname{supp}(D)=\{u\in U:D(u)\ne0\}$; $D(u)$ is the number of occurrences of record $u$. Let $\mathcal D$ be the set of databases and equip it with the power-set sigma-algebra. For $u\in U$, let $\mathbf 1_{\{u\}}$ be the function that is one at $u$ and zero elsewhere. Two databases $D,D'\in\mathcal D$ are neighbors, written $D\sim D'$, when $D'=D+\mathbf 1_{\{u\}}$ or $D=D'+\mathbf 1_{\{u\}}$ for some $u\in U$.

A randomized mechanism with output measurable space $(Y,\mathcal B)$ is a probability kernel $K$ from $\mathcal D$ to $Y$: for each $D\in\mathcal D$, $A\mapsto K(D,A)$ is a probability measure on $(Y,\mathcal B)$, and for each $A\in\mathcal B$, $D\mapsto K(D,A)$ is measurable. Given $\varepsilon\ge0$ and $0\le\delta\le1$, the mechanism is $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-differentially private if, for every ordered neighboring pair $D\sim D'$ and every output event $A\in\mathcal B$,

$$
K(D,A)\le e^{\varepsilon}K(D',A)+\delta.
$$

The mechanism is $\varepsilon$-differentially private, or pure $\varepsilon$-differentially private, when $\delta=0$. The ordered-pair quantifier includes both directions because $\sim$ is symmetric.

Let $\mathcal D$ be the finite-support count functions on a nonempty record universe, with add/remove-one-occurrence adjacency. Let $R$ be a nonempty finite set independent of the database, and let $u:\mathcal D\times R\to\mathbb R$ be a real-valued utility. When the set of adjacent-pair utility differences has an attained finite maximum, the global utility sensitivity of $u$ is
$$
\Delta_u=\max_{D\sim D',\,r\in R}|u(D,r)-u(D',r)|.
$$
The sensitivity is positive when $\Delta_u>0$; the exponential mechanism on this page uses that positive-sensitivity case.

Let $\mathcal D$ be the finite-support count functions on a nonempty record universe, with add/remove-one-occurrence adjacency. Input a database $D\in\mathcal D$, a parameter $\varepsilon>0$, a nonempty finite database-independent range $R$, and a real-valued utility $u:\mathcal D\times R\to\mathbb R$ with finite positive global utility sensitivity $\Delta_u$. For each $r\in R$, set
$$ w_D(r)=\exp\!\left(\frac{\varepsilon u(D,r)}{2\Delta_u}\right),\qquad Z_D=\sum_{s\in R}w_D(s). $$
Output $r\in R$ with probability $w_D(r)/Z_D$. Equip $R$ with its power-set sigma-algebra and define $K(D,B)=\sum_{r\in B}w_D(r)/Z_D$ for each $B\subseteq R$; this is the probability kernel from databases to outputs.

Let $\mathcal D$ be the set of finite-support record-count databases, with neighbors defined by adding or removing one record occurrence. Let $R$ be a nonempty finite set independent of the database, and let $u:\mathcal D\times R\to\mathbb R$ be a real-valued utility with finite positive attained global utility sensitivity $\Delta_u$. For $\varepsilon>0$, use weights $w_D(r)=\exp(\varepsilon u(D,r)/(2\Delta_u))$ and normalize them over $R$ as in the exponential mechanism. Its output law is $(\varepsilon,0)$-differentially private. For a fixed database $D$, let
$$ \operatorname{OPT}_u(D)=\max_{r\in R}u(D,r),\qquad R_{\operatorname{OPT}}=\{r\in R:u(D,r)=\operatorname{OPT}_u(D)\}. $$
For every $t>0$, if $M(D)$ denotes the random output, then
$$
\Pr\!\left[u(D,M(D))\le\operatorname{OPT}_u(D)-\frac{2\Delta_u}{\varepsilon}\left(\ln\frac{|R|}{|R_{\operatorname{OPT}}|}+t\right)\right]\le e^{-t}.
$$

derivations.claim: For the first utility, every score is independent of $D$, so every adjacent-pair difference is zero and $\Delta_u=0$ by [F2]. This fails the positive-sensitivity hypothesis in [F3], so the algorithm is not defined for that utility.

For the second utility, adding or removing a record other than $u_*$ leaves $s(D)$ unchanged; adding or removing $u_*$ changes it by at most one. The empty database and the database with one occurrence of $u_*$ are neighbors and change $s$ from zero to one. The score at $a$ is constant, and the score at $b$ changes by exactly the change in $s$, so the maximum adjacent score difference is attained and equals $\Delta_u=1$.

With $\Delta_u=1$, the weights are $w_D(a)=e^{\varepsilon/2}$ and $w_D(b)=e^{\varepsilon(1-s(D))/2}$. Normalizing their sum gives the displayed selection probability. Since the range is finite nonempty and the sensitivity is positive, [F4] proves the privacy claim.

Let $U$ be a nonempty record universe, let $\mathcal D$ be its finite-support count databases with add/remove-one-occurrence adjacency, let $R=\{a,b\}$, and let $\varepsilon>0$. The constant utility $u(D,a)=1$, $u(D,b)=0$ has $\Delta_u=0$, so it is inadmissible for the positive-sensitivity exponential mechanism. Fix a possible record $u_*\in U$ and define $s(D)=1$ exactly when $D(u_*)>0$. Instead set $u(D,a)=1$ and $u(D,b)=1-s(D)$. Then $\Delta_u=1$, the mechanism is $(\varepsilon,0)$-differentially private, and it selects $a$ with probability
$$
\frac{e^{\varepsilon/2}}{e^{\varepsilon/2}+e^{\varepsilon(1-s(D))/2}}.
$$

Let $(K,U,R)$ be a mirror regularizer with $R$ $m$-strongly convex on $K$ for some $m>0$. Fix an integer horizon $T\ge1$ and a step size $\eta>0$. Admissibility requires the unique minimizer of $R$ on $K$ to lie in $U$; initialize $x_1$ at this minimizer. At each round $t=1,\ldots,T$, play $x_t$ before observing the full current loss $f_t$, with losses and gradients written in the same affine coordinates used for $K$. Use either of these feedback cases:

1. $f_t$ is differentiable and convex on an open convex set containing $K$, and $g_t=\nabla f_t(x_t)$.
2. $f_t$ is convex on a convex set containing $K$, and a supplied vector $g_t$ satisfies $f_t(u)\ge f_t(x_t)+\langle g_t,u-x_t\rangle$ for every $u\in K$.

For each round require that there is a unique $y_{t+1}\in U$ satisfying

$$\nabla R(y_{t+1})=\nabla R(x_t)-\eta g_t.$$

Set $x_{t+1}$ to the minimizer of $B_R(x\|y_{t+1})$ over $x\in K$, and require this minimizer to lie in $U$ so that the next dual update is defined. The Bregman minimizer exists and is unique under the stated strong-convexity and compactness hypotheses. Output the decisions $x_1,\ldots,x_T$; the final $x_{T+1}$ is the internal post-round iterate.

Let $n\ge2$. Coordinates in $\mathbb R^{n-1}$ use the library's function-space convention: for $v\in\mathbb R^{n-1}$ and $1\le i<n$, write $v_i:=v(i-1)$. Let

$$K_n:=\{q\in\mathbb R^{n-1}:q_i\ge0\text{ for all }1\le i<n,\ \sum_{i=1}^{n-1}q_i\le1\},$$

and for $q\in K_n$ put $p_i=q_i$ for $1\le i<n$ and $p_n=1-\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}q_i$. Define $R(q)=\sum_{i=1}^np_i\log p_i$, with $0\log0:=0$. In the independent coordinates $q_1,\ldots,q_{n-1}$, $R$ is continuous on $K_n$, is twice continuously differentiable on its interior, is $1$-strongly convex in the Euclidean norm, and satisfies

$$-\log n\le R(q)\le0.$$

The minimum $-\log n$ is attained at $p_i=1/n$ for every $i$, and the maximum $0$ is attained at each vertex of the simplex.

Let $d\ge1$, let $K\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be nonempty, bounded, closed, and convex, and let $(K,U,R)$ be a mirror regularizer with $R$ $m$-strongly convex on $K$ for some $m>0$. Then $R$ has a unique minimizer on $K$, and for every $y\in U$ the function $x\mapsto B_R(x\|y)$ has a unique minimizer $x_+(y)$ on $K$. If $x_+(y)\in U$, then for every $u\in K$,

$$\langle\nabla R(x_+(y))-\nabla R(y),u-x_+(y)\rangle\ge0$$

and

$$B_R(u\|y)\ge B_R(u\|x_+(y))+B_R(x_+(y)\|y).$$

$$B_R(x\|y)\ge0,$$

with strict inequality when $x\ne y$. For $x\in K$ and $y\in K\cap U$,

Let $N,T\ge1$ be integers, let $[N]=\{1,\ldots,N\}$ be the expert set, and let $\epsilon>0$. At each round $t=1,\ldots,T$, a finite loss vector $\ell_t=(\ell_t(1),\ldots,\ell_t(N))\in[0,\infty)^N$ is revealed after the learner's choice. Initialize $W_1(i)=1$ for every $i\in[N]$. At round $t$, set
$$x_t(i):=\frac{W_t(i)}{\sum_{j=1}^{N}W_t(j)},\qquad i\in[N],$$
Let $\mathcal H_{t-1}$ be the pre-round history sigma-algebra generated by the previously played choices and all previously revealed loss vectors (any random loss vector is assumed measurable on the protocol's probability space). The weights and $x_t$ are $\mathcal H_{t-1}$-measurable. Draw a measurable expert choice $I_t\in[N]$ with conditional distribution
$$\mathbb P(I_t=i\mid\mathcal H_{t-1})=x_t(i)\quad\text{almost surely},\qquad i\in[N],$$
and play $I_t$. After observing the whole vector $\ell_t$, update
$$W_{t+1}(i):=W_t(i)\exp(-\epsilon\ell_t(i)),\qquad i\in[N].$$
The output is the distributions $x_1,\ldots,x_T$, the sampled choices $I_1,\ldots,I_T$, and the final weights. The protocol assumes a probability space carrying the stated measurable draws; no probability-space construction is claimed.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

derivations.claim: On $U_n$, differentiating $R(q)=\sum_{i<n}q_i\log q_i+p_n\log p_n$ using [F6, F9] gives $\partial_iR=\log q_i+1-(\log p_n+1)=\log(q_i/p_n)$ and $\nabla^2R(q)=\operatorname{diag}(1/q_1,\ldots,1/q_{n-1})+\frac1{p_n}\mathbf1\mathbf1^\top$. For every nonzero $v$, $v^\top\nabla^2R(q)v=\sum_{i<n}v_i^2/q_i+(\sum_{i<n}v_i)^2/p_n>0$. Thus the Hessian is positive definite on $U_n$; together with [F2] and [F10], this verifies the mirror-regularizer conditions for $(K_n,U_n)$ and the validity of the uniform initialization.

In independent coordinates the linear loss is $f_t(q)=\ell_{t,n}+\sum_{i<n}q_i(\ell_{t,i}-\ell_{t,n})$, so its gradient has coordinates $g_{t,i}=\ell_{t,i}-\ell_{t,n}$. The dual equation [F1] therefore reads $\log(p_{t+1,i}/p_{t+1,n})=\log(p_{t,i}/p_{t,n})-\eta(\ell_{t,i}-\ell_{t,n})$ by the quotient law [F7].

By [F7, F8], $\exp$ is multiplicative: for real $a,b$, $\log(\exp(a)\exp(b))=a+b=\log(\exp(a+b))$, so injectivity of $\log$ gives $\exp(a+b)=\exp(a)\exp(b)$. Also $\exp(0)=1$ by $\log1=0$ and [F8], hence $\exp(-b)=1/\exp(b)$. Any positive normalized solution of step 1.2 therefore satisfies $p_{t+1,i}/p_{t+1,n}=(p_{t,i}/p_{t,n})\exp(-\eta\ell_{t,i})/\exp(-\eta\ell_{t,n})$. It follows that its coordinates have the form $c_t p_{t,i}\exp(-\eta\ell_{t,i})$ for a common $c_t>0$, and normalization forces $c_t=(\sum_jp_{t,j}\exp(-\eta\ell_{t,j}))^{-1}$. Conversely, define the candidate by this normalized formula. Its denominator is a finite positive real by [F8], and [F7] together with $\log(\exp z)=z$ from [F8] verifies that it satisfies the dual equation in step 1.2. Thus the dual point exists uniquely and is exactly the displayed update.

The denominator in step 2.1 is a finite sum of positive finite terms, so each updated coordinate is positive and the update lies in the simplex interior. By [F4], the Bregman objective is nonnegative on the simplex and equals zero at this update point itself; hence the Bregman projection returns this same point.

At initialization, [F2] and [F10] make the uniform distribution a minimizer of $R$ in $U_n$, so it is a valid OMD initial point. If $p_t(i)=W_t(i)/\sum_jW_t(j)$ and $\epsilon=\eta$, then [F5] gives $W_{t+1}(i)=W_t(i)\exp(-\eta\ell_{t,i})$, whose normalization is exactly the update in step 2.1. Induction from $W_1(i)=1$ proves equality of the OMD and Hedge distributions at every round.

citations.quote: Let $S$ be a finite nonempty state set and let $A(s)$ be a finite nonempty action set for each $s\in S$, as in the finite-MDP convention. Put $D=\{(s,a):s\in S,\ a\in A(s)\}$ with its discrete sigma-algebra. Equip $S$ with its power-set sigma-algebra, $[0,1]$ with its Borel sigma-algebra, and $S\times[0,1]$ with the product sigma-algebra. A finite MDP with bounded real rewards specifies a probability kernel $Q$ from $D$ to $S\times[0,1]$; equivalently, each admissible $(s,a)$ has a probability measure $Q(\cdot\mid s,a)$ on that product measurable space. The reward-coordinate projection $(s',\rho)\mapsto\rho$ is measurable because the preimage of each Borel set $B\subseteq[0,1]$ is the product rectangle $S\times B$. Define the next-state law by $P(s'\mid s,a)=Q(\{s'\}\times[0,1]\mid s,a)$ and the mean reward by $r(s,a)=\int_{S\times[0,1]}\rho\,Q(ds',d\rho\mid s,a)\in[0,1]$. At each time, conditional on the observed history and the selected action, the next-state/reward pair has this law. Assume the Axiom of Choice for the path-space construction under policies.

Assume the Axiom of Choice for the policy path laws used in the expectations below. For a finite MDP with bounded rewards, a policy assigns a probability distribution on $A(s)$ to each finite observed history ending in state $s$, with each action probability a measurable function of the history; deterministic policies are included. For states $x,y$, start at $S_0=x$ and define $\tau_y=\inf\{t\ge0:S_t=y\}$, with $\tau_y=+\infty$ if $y$ is never hit. This is an extended nonnegative measurable random variable because $\{\tau_y\le n\}=\bigcup_{t=0}^n\{S_t=y\}$. Take the expectation and the infimum over policies in $[0,+\infty]$. The MDP is communicating if $\inf_\pi\mathbb E_x^\pi[\tau_y]<\infty$ for every ordered pair $(x,y)$. Its raw diameter is $D_0=\sup_{x,y}\inf_\pi\mathbb E_x^\pi[\tau_y]$ in $[0,+\infty]$, and its normalized diameter is $D=\max\{1,D_0\}$ in the extended order. Since $S$ is finite, $D_0$ is finite for every communicating MDP. Thus a one-state MDP has $D_0=0$ and $D=1$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $k,T$ be positive integers, let $\eta>0$, and let $[k]=\{1,\ldots,k\}$. The input also supplies a full-information loss process: before the round-$t$ action draw, its vector $\ell_t\in[0,1]^k$ is fixed using only the previous transcript and any external randomness, and the vector is revealed after the draw. Put $H_t=([k]\times[0,1]^k)^{t-1}$, with $H_1=\{()\}$, and give $H_t$ its power-set sigma-algebra; these histories have finite length but need not be finite sets. Initialize $w_{1,j}=1$ for each $j\in[k]$. At round $t$, given $h_{t-1}=((a_s,\ell_s))_{s<t}$, compute
$$p_{t,j}=\frac{w_{t,j}}{\sum_{r=1}^k w_{t,r}}.$$
Draw $a_t=j$ with probability $p_{t,j}$, observe the entire vector $\ell_t$, and update $w_{t+1,j}=w_{t,j}\exp(-\eta\ell_t(j))$. Equivalently, the conditional action kernel is $K_t(h_{t-1},A)=\sum_{j\in A}p_{t,j}$ for each $A\subseteq[k]$. The action draw uses fresh randomness independent of the loss process, so its conditional law given the past and the already fixed current loss vector is $K_t$. Return the action transcript $(a_1,\ldots,a_T)$.

Let $k,T\ge1$ be integers, let $[k]=\{1,\ldots,k\}$, let $\eta>0$, and let each loss vector lie in $[0,1]^k$. Before round $t$ define $w_{t,j}=\exp(-\eta\sum_{s<t}\ell_s(j))$, $W_t=\sum_{i=1}^k w_{t,i}$, and $p_{t,j}=w_{t,j}/W_t$. Draw $a_t=j$ with probability $p_{t,j}$, then observe the full vector $\ell_t$ and update $w_{t+1,j}=w_{t,j}\exp(-\eta\ell_t(j))$; release the transcript $(a_1,\ldots,a_T)$. For the regret claims, assume a filtered probability model $(\Omega,\mathcal F,(\mathcal F_t)_{t=0}^T,\mathbb P)$ in which $\ell_t$ and $p_t$ are $\mathcal F_{t-1}$-measurable, each action $a_t$ is $\mathcal F_t$-measurable, and $\mathbb P(a_t=j\mid\mathcal F_{t-1})=p_{t,j}$ for every $j\in[k]$; hence each prior action is $\mathcal F_{t-1}$-measurable and the loss vector may depend on the previous transcript but not on the current draw. Set
$$R_T=\frac1T\sum_{t=1}^T\ell_t(a_t)-\min_{j\in[k]}\frac1T\sum_{t=1}^T\ell_t(j).$$
Then
$$\mathbb E R_T\le \eta+\frac{\ln k}{\eta T},$$
for every such process. Assuming the Axiom of Choice, for every $0<\beta<1$,
$$\Pr\!\left(R_T\le \eta+\frac{\ln k}{\eta T}+\sqrt{\frac{\ln(1/\beta)}{2T}}\right)\ge1-\beta.$$
The expected-regret proof uses no choice axiom. At $k=1$, $R_T=0$ identically. For $k\ge2$, substituting $\eta=\sqrt{\ln k/T}$ into the expected-regret bound gives $2\sqrt{\ln k/T}$.

For privacy, let $\mathcal L_T:=([0,1]^k)^T$ carry the power-set sigma-algebra, regard a fixed sequence $(\ell_1,\ldots,\ell_T)\in\mathcal L_T$ as the input, and make two sequences adjacent when one complete time-step vector is replaced by an arbitrary vector in $[0,1]^k$. Give the full action transcript $[k]^T$ its power-set sigma-algebra. For every common prior action history, the round-$t$ action kernels satisfy the ordered event inequalities for $(2\eta,0)$-differential privacy. Assuming the Axiom of Choice, for every $\varepsilon>0$ and $0<\delta<1$, put $L=\ln(1/\delta)$ and choose
$$\eta=\min\left\{\frac{\varepsilon}{\sqrt{32TL}},\frac12,\sqrt{\frac{\varepsilon}{16T}}\right\}.$$
The full transcript is then $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-differentially private. With this choice the high-probability bound above is exactly
$$R_T\le \eta+\frac{\ln k}{T} \max\left\{\frac{\sqrt{32TL}}{\varepsilon},\,2,\,4\sqrt{\frac{T}{\varepsilon}}\right\} +\sqrt{\frac{\ln(1/\beta)}{2T}}$$
with probability at least $1-\beta$. If $\eta_0=\varepsilon/\sqrt{32TL}$ satisfies $\varepsilon\le\sqrt{8TL}$ and $\varepsilon\le2L$, then $\eta=\eta_0$ and this bound specializes to
$$R_T\le \eta_0+\frac{\sqrt{32L}\,\ln k}{\varepsilon\sqrt T} +\sqrt{\frac{\ln(1/\beta)}{2T}}.$$
The fixed-sequence privacy claim and the nonanticipating adaptive-loss regret claim have distinct input quantifiers. The same privacy conclusion applies on any set of interactive loss-generating strategies equipped with its power-set sigma-algebra and a symmetric adjacency relation, provided that, for each strategy, its action kernels are measurable in the prior transcript and, at every common transcript, they satisfy the ordered $(2\eta,0)$ event inequalities for every ordered adjacent pair of strategies.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $S$ be a finite set, possibly empty, let $\mathcal R$ be a finite subset of $\mathbb R$, and for each $s\in S$ let $A(s)$ be a finite nonempty set. Here **finite** means bijective with a natural number, and the **discrete sigma-algebra** on a set is its power set. Write $D=\{(s,a):s\in S,\ a\in A(s)\}$. A **finite Markov decision process (MDP)** consists of these sets and numbers $p(s',\rho\mid s,a)\in[0,1]$, indexed by $(s,a)\in D$, $s'\in S$, and $\rho\in\mathcal R$, with

$$ \sum_{s'\in S}\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal R}p(s',\rho\mid s,a)=1 \qquad ((s,a)\in D). $$

Equip each set used here, including $D$, with its power-set (discrete) sigma-algebra. Thus $p$ is the point-mass form of a probability kernel from $D$ to $S\times\mathcal R$: each input assigns a probability measure on $S\times\mathcal R$, and every event section is measurable. The joint law allows the next state and reward to be dependent. Define the expected reward and state-transition probabilities by

$$ r(s,a)=\sum_{s'\in S}\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal R}\rho\,p(s',\rho\mid s,a), \qquad P(s'\mid s,a)=\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal R}p(s',\rho\mid s,a). $$

If $\mathcal R\ne\emptyset$, put $M=\max_{\rho\in\mathcal R}|\rho|$; if $\mathcal R=\emptyset$, put $M=0$. A stationary Markov policy is a family of probabilities $\pi(a\mid s)\ge0$ with $\sum_{a\in A(s)}\pi(a\mid s)=1$ for every $s\in S$. A deterministic policy is a function $\pi$ with $\pi(s)\in A(s)$ for every $s$. When $S=\emptyset$, these families and policies are the unique empty functions and all statewise formulas are vacuous.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let a finite MDP have nonempty state set $S$, and let $\pi$ be a stationary Markov policy. Fix an initial state $s_0\in S$ and let

$$Z=\{(s,a,r,s'):s\in S,\ a\in A(s),\ r\in\mathcal R,\ s'\in S\}$$

with its discrete sigma-algebra. There is a probability law on $S\times Z^{\mathbb N}$ whose first state is $S_0=s_0$ and whose subsequent coordinates are $Z_n=(S_n,A_n,R_{n+1},S_{n+1})$. For every $m\ge0$ and every feasible finite trajectory $(s_0,a_0,r_1,s_1,\ldots,a_{m-1},r_m,s_m)$, its probability is

$$
\prod_{n=0}^{m-1}\pi(a_n\mid s_n)\,p(s_{n+1},r_{n+1}\mid s_n,a_n),
$$

where the empty product for $m=0$ is $1$.

Its state-reward marginal also has the finite-prefix probabilities

$$
\prod_{n=0}^{m-1}\sum_{a\in A(s_n)}\pi(a\mid s_n)p(s_{n+1},r_{n+1}\mid s_n,a)
$$

for each feasible finite state-reward path $(s_0,r_1,s_1,\ldots,r_m,s_m)$.

Let a finite MDP have $0\le\gamma<1$ and let $S_\dagger\subseteq S$ be a set of terminal states. Form an absorbing extension with reward alphabet $\mathcal R^\dagger=\mathcal R\cup\{0\}$: from each nonterminal state retain the original joint reward-transition law, and from each terminal state use the deterministic transition back to that state with reward zero. Assume AC for the path laws defining policy values. For a stationary policy $\sigma$, an episode starting from $s$ ends at its first hitting time $T=\inf\{n\ge0:S_n\in S_\dagger\}$; require $T<\infty$ almost surely under every policy used. The return from time $t<T$ is

$$
G_t=\sum_{k=t}^{T-1}\gamma^{k-t}R_{k+1},
$$

and $G_T=0$. This equals the infinite discounted return of the absorbing extension, whose state value is $V^\sigma(s)=\mathbb E_{\sigma,s}[G_0]$.

For a state-value estimate $V_n$, the state temporal-difference error on a transition is $\delta_n^V=R_{n+1}+\gamma V_n(S_{n+1})-V_n(S_n)$. For an action-value estimate $Q_n$, the sampled-action Sarsa error is $\delta_n^{\mathrm{Sarsa}}=R_{n+1}+\gamma Q_n(S_{n+1},A_{n+1})-Q_n(S_n,A_n)$, and the greedy Q-learning error is $\delta_n^{Q}=R_{n+1}+\gamma\max_{b\in A(S_{n+1})}Q_n(S_{n+1},b)-Q_n(S_n,A_n)$. In each error, the continuation term is defined as zero when $S_{n+1}$ is terminal.

In off-policy prediction, $\mu$ denotes the behavior policy generating episodes and $\pi$ the target policy whose value is estimated. Target support means $\pi(a\mid s)>0$ implies $\mu(a\mid s)>0$ for every state-action pair that can be visited. For a behavior-generated episode, the state-return likelihood ratio from time $t$ is

$$
\Lambda_{t:T-1}=\prod_{k=t}^{T-1}\frac{\pi(A_k\mid S_k)}{\mu(A_k\mid S_k)}.
$$

Each denominator is positive on the observed behavior path. When estimating a value conditional on an already fixed action $A_t$, the first factor begins at time $t+1$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let a finite MDP with terminal set $S_\dagger$ have $0\le\gamma<1$, and let $\pi$ and $\mu$ be stationary target and behavior policies. Suppose $\pi(a\mid x)>0$ implies $\mu(a\mid x)>0$ for every nonterminal state $x$ and action $a\in A(x)$, and episodes reach $S_\dagger$ in finite time almost surely from every state under both policies. For any starting state $s$, a behavior-generated episode has first terminal time $T$ and ratio

$$
\Lambda_{0:T-1}=\prod_{k=0}^{T-1}\frac{\pi(A_k\mid S_k)}{\mu(A_k\mid S_k)},
$$

where the empty product for $T=0$ is $1$. For every bounded measurable real function $G$ of the finite episode,

$$
E_{\mu,s}[\Lambda_{0:T-1}G]=E_{\pi,s}[G].
$$

The identity therefore applies to every episode suffix starting at a state $s$ that can be reached by a finite behavior history. Fix an initial state $s_0$. If $H$ is a positive-probability finite behavior history from $s_0$ that first visits $s$ at time $t$ and ends immediately upon observing $S_t=s$, before the action $A_t$ is sampled (when $s$ is terminal, no action is sampled and the suffix is empty), let

$$G_t=\sum_{k=t}^{T-1}\gamma^{k-t}R_{k+1}$$

be the suffix return. Then

$$
\frac{E_{\mu,s_0}[\mathbf1_H\Lambda_{t:T-1}G_t]}{P_{\mu,s_0}(H)}=V^\pi(s).
$$

Thus the ordinary first-visit importance-sampling return has mean $V^\pi(s)$ conditional on each pre-action first-visit history.

Let $r \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $r^k$ be the integer power ([[def-integer-power]]),
so that $r^0 = 1$ for every $r$, including $r = 0$.

1. If $|r| < 1$ then the series $\sum r^k$ converges ([[def-series]]) and
   $$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} r^{k} \;=\; \frac{1}{1-r} .$$
2. If $|r| \ge 1$ then $\sum r^k$ diverges.

The series starts at $k = 0$ and its first term is $r^0 = 1$; in particular
$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} 2^{-k} = 2$, while the series starting at $k = 1$ sums to
$1$. Which starting index is meant has to be said, and it is said here.

Let $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be a decreasing sequence of measurable sets for a measure $\mu$. If $\mu(E_{n_0})<+\infty$ for some $n_0$, then

$$\mu\left(\bigcap_{n\in\mathbb N}E_n\right)=\inf_{n\in\mathbb N}\mu(E_n).$$

A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ ([[def-measure]]). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** ([[def-measure-space]]); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

- If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, its **expectation** is the
  extended-valued integral
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P\in[0,+\infty].$$
- If $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ or $X:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is integrable in the sense
  of [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], its
  **expectation** is again
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P,$$
  now a finite real or complex number.

For an integrable real random variable,
$$\mathbb E[X]=\mathbb E[X^+]-\mathbb E[X^-],$$
where $X^+$ and $X^-$ are its positive and negative parts.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

derivations.claim: Under $\mu$, the event $\{N\ge n\}$ consists of $n$ successive choices of $a$ and has probability $(1/10)^n$ by [F2]. Under $\pi$ it has probability $(1/2)^n$. These events decrease to the event of never choosing $b$; [F6] shows that this event has probability zero under either policy. Since both actions have positive probability under both policies, target support holds.

Under $\pi$, $P_\pi(N=n)=2^{-(n+1)}$ and the return on that episode is $(9/10)^n$. Summing first over $N\le m$ and then letting $m\to\infty$, [F7]–[F8] and [F5] give $V^\pi(s)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}2^{-(n+1)}(9/10)^n =\frac12\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}(9/20)^n=\frac{10}{11}.$ For the episode with $N=n$, the likelihood ratio is $5^n(5/9)$ and hence $X_n=(5/9)(9/2)^n$. By [F4] and the support and termination verified in step 1.1, $E_\mu[X]=V^\pi(s)=10/11$.

The behavior probability of $N=n$ is $(9/10)(1/10)^n$. Therefore $E_\mu[X^2]=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac9{10}\left(\frac1{10}\right)^n\left[\frac59\left(\frac92\right)^n\right]^2 =\frac5{18}\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\left(\frac{81}{40}\right)^n=+\infty,$ where [F7]–[F8] justify the nonnegative path sum and [F5] gives divergence because $81/40>1$. Let $m=10/11$. Since $X_n\to\infty$, there is $n_0$ such that $X_n\ge2m$ for all $n\ge n_0$, and then $(X_n-m)^2\ge X_n^2/4$. The tail second moment is infinite, so $E_\mu[(X-m)^2]=+\infty$. Together with the finite mean from step 2.1, this proves that $X$ has infinite variance.

**Input:** A bounded-reward finite discounted MDP interaction, its discount $0\le\gamma<1$, an admissible upper heuristic $U$ with cap $V_{\max}$, an integer batch size $m\ge1$, a bonus $0<\epsilon_1<1$, and a fixed total order on each action set.

**Output:** At each interaction time $t$, the selected action $a_t$. The table $Q$, batch sums, sample counts, batch-start times, learning flags, and global last-update time are internal state; the procedure does not return them as outputs.

Initialize $Q(s,a)=U(s,a)$, batch sum $B(s,a)=0$, sample count $\ell(s,a)=0$, batch start $b(s,a)=0$, learning flag $L(s,a)=\mathrm{true}$, and global last-update time $t^*=0$. For interaction times $t=1,2,\ldots$, in current state $s$, choose an action maximizing $Q(s,\cdot)$ under the fixed tie order, output and take that action $a_t$, then observe reward $r$ and next state $s'$. If $b(s,a)\le t^*$, set $L(s,a)=\mathrm{true}$. If $L(s,a)$ is true, set $b(s,a)=t$ when $\ell(s,a)=0$, increment $\ell(s,a)$ by one, and add $r+\gamma\max_{c\in A(s')}Q(s',c)$ to $B(s,a)$. When $\ell(s,a)=m$, set $\bar B=B(s,a)/m$. If $Q(s,a)-\bar B\ge2\epsilon_1$, replace $Q(s,a)$ by $\bar B+\epsilon_1$ and set $t^*=t$. Otherwise set $L(s,a)=\mathrm{false}$ exactly when $b(s,a)>t^*$. In either outcome reset $B(s,a)=0$ and $\ell(s,a)=0$ after a completed batch; if $L(s,a)$ remains false, make no sample or Q update on this visit. Leave all other entries unchanged. Use $s'$ as the current state in the next iteration.

For a bounded-reward finite discounted MDP, an **admissible upper heuristic** is a function $U:D\to[0,V_0]$ such that $Q^*(s,a)\le U(s,a)$ for every admissible pair and a supplied scalar satisfies $0\le V_0\le(1-\gamma)^{-1}$. Define the effective reward-scale cap $V_{\max}=\max\{1,V_0\}$. Then $U(s,a)\le V_{\max}\le(1-\gamma)^{-1}$. The floor at $1$ is part of this convention because an observed reward can lie anywhere in $[0,1]$, even when the heuristic values are all smaller than $1$.

Let $M$ be a bounded-reward finite discounted MDP, write $S=|S|$ and $A=\max_s|A(s)|$, and fix $0\le\epsilon<(1-\gamma)^{-1}$, $0<\delta<1$, and an admissible heuristic with normalized cap $V_{\max}$. At $\epsilon=0$, if $V^*(s)=0$ at every state then $N_0=0$; no finite zero-tolerance extension holds uniformly over this class: already at $\gamma=0$, every fixed finite legal batch size $m$ and bonus $\epsilon_1$ admits an admissible one-state example for Delayed Q-learning with $N_0=\infty$ with positive probability. This does not assert failure for every fixed heuristic or model. The parameter formulas below are evaluated only when $\epsilon>0$. Assume now $\epsilon>0$. If $\epsilon\ge V_{\max}$, then $N_\epsilon=0$. Otherwise put
$$\eta=\epsilon/4,\quad \epsilon_1=\frac{\eta(1-\gamma)}3,\quad \kappa=\left\lceil\frac{SA V_{\max}}{\epsilon_1}\right\rceil,\quad N=SA(1+\kappa),\quad C_1=1+\gamma V_{\max},$$
and choose
$$m=\left\lceil\frac{C_1^2}{2\epsilon_1^2}\ln\frac{16N}{\delta}\right\rceil.$$
Run Delayed Q-learning with $m$ and $\epsilon_1$. Write $D(s,a)=[U(s,a)-V^*(s)]_+$, $G=\sum_{s,a}(1+D(s,a)/\epsilon_1)$, and $\zeta=\lceil(2m+1)G\rceil$. Define $q,H,M$ by
$$q=\frac{\eta}{4V_{\max}},\qquad H=\begin{cases}1,&\gamma=0,\\ \max\{1,\lceil\ln(1/[\eta(1-\gamma)])/(-\ln\gamma)\rceil\},&0<\gamma<1,\end{cases}\qquad M=\left\lceil\frac{2(\zeta+1)+2\ln(2/\delta)}q\right\rceil.$$
Then $\mathbb P(N_\epsilon\le HM)\ge1-\delta$. Equivalently, up to logarithmic factors, the bound is
$$\widetilde O\!\left(\frac{V_{\max}(1+\gamma V_{\max})^2\left[\sum_{s,a}D(s,a)+SA\epsilon(1-\gamma)\right]}{\epsilon^4(1-\gamma)^4}\right),$$
where $\widetilde O$ suppresses logarithmic factors. The additive term remains when all heuristic slacks vanish. For $V_{\max}=(1-\gamma)^{-1}$ this gives $\widetilde O(SA/[\epsilon^4(1-\gamma)^8])$.


For every $\epsilon>0$, a bound uniform over all MDPs and admissible heuristics with these $S,A,\gamma$ is obtained by setting
$$\bar V=\frac1{1-\gamma},\quad \bar\epsilon_1=\frac{\epsilon(1-\gamma)}{12},\quad \bar\kappa=\left\lceil\frac{SA\bar V}{\bar\epsilon_1}\right\rceil,\quad \bar N=SA(1+\bar\kappa),$$
$$\bar m=\left\lceil\frac{\bar V^2}{2\bar\epsilon_1^2}\ln\frac{16\bar N}{\delta}\right\rceil,\quad \bar G=SA\left(1+\frac{\bar V}{\bar\epsilon_1}\right),\quad \bar\zeta=\left\lceil(2\bar m+1)\bar G\right\rceil,\quad \bar q=\frac{\epsilon(1-\gamma)}{16},$$
and
$$\bar H=\begin{cases}1,&\gamma=0,\\ \max\{1,\lceil\ln(1/[(\epsilon/4)(1-\gamma)])/(-\ln\gamma)\rceil\},&0<\gamma<1,\end{cases}\qquad \bar M=\left\lceil\frac{2(\bar\zeta+1)+2\ln(2/\delta)}{\bar q}\right\rceil.$$ 
Then $\mathbb P(N_\epsilon\le\bar H\bar M)\ge1-\delta$. This bound depends only on $S,A,\epsilon,\delta,\gamma$.

derivations.claim: Initially $Q(s,a)=Q(s,b)=1$, so the tie order selects $b$. Since $\gamma=0$, each of its first $m$ targets is its observed reward $0$; no update occurs before the batch completes. At the $m$th sample the mean is $0$, so $Q(s,b)-0=1\ge2\epsilon_1$ and [F1] updates it to $\epsilon_1<1$.

The other action remains at value $1$, so the next greedy action is $a$. Also $V^*(s)=1$ and both heuristic values equal $1$, hence every $D(s,a)=0$ and their sum is zero. citations.quote: For a bounded-reward finite discounted MDP, an **admissible upper heuristic** is a function $U:D\to[0,V_0]$ such that $Q^*(s,a)\le U(s,a)$ for every admissible pair and a supplied scalar satisfies $0\le V_0\le(1-\gamma)^{-1}$. Define the effective reward-scale cap $V_{\max}=\max\{1,V_0\}$. Then $U(s,a)\le V_{\max}\le(1-\gamma)^{-1}$. The floor at $1$ is part of this convention because an observed reward can lie anywhere in $[0,1]$, even when the heuristic values are all smaller than $1$.

Let $M$ be a bounded-reward finite discounted MDP, write $S=|S|$ and $A=\max_s|A(s)|$, and fix $0\le\epsilon<(1-\gamma)^{-1}$, $0<\delta<1$, and an admissible heuristic with normalized cap $V_{\max}$. At $\epsilon=0$, if $V^*(s)=0$ at every state then $N_0=0$; no finite zero-tolerance extension holds uniformly over this class: already at $\gamma=0$, every fixed finite legal sample threshold $m$ and value-iteration tolerance $\beta$ admits an admissible one-state example for R-MAX with $N_0=\infty$ with positive probability. This does not assert failure for every fixed heuristic or model. The parameter formulas below are evaluated only when $\epsilon>0$. Assume now $\epsilon>0$. If $\epsilon\ge V_{\max}$, then $N_\epsilon=0$. Otherwise put
$$\eta=\epsilon/4,\quad b=\frac{\eta(1-\gamma)}{64V_{\max}},\quad m=\left\lceil\frac{8(S+\ln(16SA/\delta))}{b^2}\right\rceil,\quad \beta=\frac{\eta(1-\gamma)}{16},$$
and run R-MAX with sample threshold $m$ and value-iteration tolerance $\beta$. Let $E_\eta=\{(s,a):U(s,a)\ge V^*(s)-\eta\}$ and $\zeta=(m+1)|E_\eta|$. Define $q=\eta/(4V_{\max})$, and define $H$ and $M$ by
$$H=\begin{cases}1,&\gamma=0,\\ \max\{1,\lceil\ln(1/[\eta(1-\gamma)])/(-\ln\gamma)\rceil\},&0<\gamma<1,\end{cases}\qquad M=\left\lceil\frac{2(\zeta+1)+2\ln(2/\delta)}q\right\rceil.$$
Then $\mathbb P(N_\epsilon\le HM)\ge1-\delta$. For the uninformative heuristic $U(s,a)=V_{\max}=(1-\gamma)^{-1}$, the bound is $\widetilde O(S^2A/[\epsilon^3(1-\gamma)^6])$, where $\widetilde O$ suppresses logarithmic factors.


For every $\epsilon>0$, a bound uniform over all MDPs and admissible heuristics with these $S,A,\gamma$ is obtained by setting
$$\bar V=\frac1{1-\gamma},\quad \bar b=\frac{\epsilon(1-\gamma)^2}{256},\quad \bar m=\left\lceil\frac{8(S+\ln(16SA/\delta))}{\bar b^2}\right\rceil,\quad \bar q=\frac{\epsilon(1-\gamma)}{16},\quad \bar\zeta=(\bar m+1)SA,$$
and
$$\bar H=\begin{cases}1,&\gamma=0,\\ \max\{1,\lceil\ln(1/[(\epsilon/4)(1-\gamma)])/(-\ln\gamma)\rceil\},&0<\gamma<1,\end{cases}\qquad \bar M=\left\lceil\frac{2(\bar\zeta+1)+2\ln(2/\delta)}{\bar q}\right\rceil.$$ 
Then $\mathbb P(N_\epsilon\le\bar H\bar M)\ge1-\delta$. This bound depends only on $S,A,\epsilon,\delta,\gamma$.

Let $M$ be a bounded-reward finite discounted MDP, write $S=|S|$ and $A=\max_s|A(s)|$, and fix $0\le\epsilon<(1-\gamma)^{-1}$, $0<\delta<1$, and an admissible heuristic with normalized cap $V_{\max}$. At $\epsilon=0$, if $V^*(s)=0$ at every state then $N_0=0$; no finite zero-tolerance extension holds uniformly over this class: already at $\gamma=0$, every fixed finite legal batch size $m$ and bonus $\epsilon_1$ admits an admissible one-state example for Delayed Q-learning with $N_0=\infty$ with positive probability. This does not assert failure for every fixed heuristic or model. The parameter formulas below are evaluated only when $\epsilon>0$. Assume now $\epsilon>0$. If $\epsilon\ge V_{\max}$, then $N_\epsilon=0$. Otherwise put
$$\eta=\epsilon/4,\quad \epsilon_1=\frac{\eta(1-\gamma)}3,\quad \kappa=\left\lceil\frac{SA V_{\max}}{\epsilon_1}\right\rceil,\quad N=SA(1+\kappa),\quad C_1=1+\gamma V_{\max},$$
and choose
$$m=\left\lceil\frac{C_1^2}{2\epsilon_1^2}\ln\frac{16N}{\delta}\right\rceil.$$
Run Delayed Q-learning with $m$ and $\epsilon_1$. Write $D(s,a)=[U(s,a)-V^*(s)]_+$, $G=\sum_{s,a}(1+D(s,a)/\epsilon_1)$, and $\zeta=\lceil(2m+1)G\rceil$. Define $q,H,M$ by
$$q=\frac{\eta}{4V_{\max}},\qquad H=\begin{cases}1,&\gamma=0,\\ \max\{1,\lceil\ln(1/[\eta(1-\gamma)])/(-\ln\gamma)\rceil\},&0<\gamma<1,\end{cases}\qquad M=\left\lceil\frac{2(\zeta+1)+2\ln(2/\delta)}q\right\rceil.$$
Then $\mathbb P(N_\epsilon\le HM)\ge1-\delta$. Equivalently, up to logarithmic factors, the bound is
$$\widetilde O\!\left(\frac{V_{\max}(1+\gamma V_{\max})^2\left[\sum_{s,a}D(s,a)+SA\epsilon(1-\gamma)\right]}{\epsilon^4(1-\gamma)^4}\right),$$
where $\widetilde O$ suppresses logarithmic factors. The additive term remains when all heuristic slacks vanish. For $V_{\max}=(1-\gamma)^{-1}$ this gives $\widetilde O(SA/[\epsilon^4(1-\gamma)^8])$.


For every $\epsilon>0$, a bound uniform over all MDPs and admissible heuristics with these $S,A,\gamma$ is obtained by setting
$$\bar V=\frac1{1-\gamma},\quad \bar\epsilon_1=\frac{\epsilon(1-\gamma)}{12},\quad \bar\kappa=\left\lceil\frac{SA\bar V}{\bar\epsilon_1}\right\rceil,\quad \bar N=SA(1+\bar\kappa),$$
$$\bar m=\left\lceil\frac{\bar V^2}{2\bar\epsilon_1^2}\ln\frac{16\bar N}{\delta}\right\rceil,\quad \bar G=SA\left(1+\frac{\bar V}{\bar\epsilon_1}\right),\quad \bar\zeta=\left\lceil(2\bar m+1)\bar G\right\rceil,\quad \bar q=\frac{\epsilon(1-\gamma)}{16},$$
and
$$\bar H=\begin{cases}1,&\gamma=0,\\ \max\{1,\lceil\ln(1/[(\epsilon/4)(1-\gamma)])/(-\ln\gamma)\rceil\},&0<\gamma<1,\end{cases}\qquad \bar M=\left\lceil\frac{2(\bar\zeta+1)+2\ln(2/\delta)}{\bar q}\right\rceil.$$ 
Then $\mathbb P(N_\epsilon\le\bar H\bar M)\ge1-\delta$. This bound depends only on $S,A,\epsilon,\delta,\gamma$.

**Input:** A bounded-reward finite discounted MDP interaction, its discount $0\le\gamma<1$, an admissible upper heuristic $U$ with cap $V_{\max}$, an integer sample threshold $m\ge1$, a value-iteration error tolerance $0<\beta<(1-\gamma)^{-1}$, and a fixed total order on each finite action set. Write $\ln$ for the natural logarithm.

**Output:** At each interaction time $t$, the selected action $a_t$. The action-value table $Q$, known set, sample lists, and empirical model are internal state; the procedure does not return $Q$ as an output.

Initialize each pair as unknown, set $Q(s,a)=U(s,a)$, and give each pair an empty list of observed rewards and next states. For interaction times $t=1,2,\ldots$, in the current state choose a maximizing action using the fixed tie order, output and take that action $a_t$, and observe reward $R_{t+1}$ and next state $S_{t+1}$. If the pair is unknown, append this observation until its list has length $m$. When it reaches $m$, mark the pair known, set its empirical reward to the sample mean and its empirical transition law to the sample frequencies. Rebuild all action values by setting the working table $Q^{(0)}(s,a)=0$, then for $j=0,\ldots,L-1$ setting $Q^{(j+1)}=H_KQ^{(j)}$, and finally replacing $Q$ by $Q^{(L)}$, for the operator
$$H_KQ(s,a)=\begin{cases}\widehat r(s,a)+\gamma\sum_{s'}\widehat P(s'\mid s,a)\max_{b\in A(s')}Q(s',b),&(s,a)\in K,\\ U(s,a),&(s,a)\notin K,\end{cases}$$
where $K$ is the current known set and
$$L=\max\!\left\{1,\left\lceil\frac{\ln(1/[\beta(1-\gamma)])}{1-\gamma}\right\rceil\right\}.$$
Pairs and their samples are never removed from $K$ or discarded. After processing the observation and any rebuild, use the observed $S_{t+1}$ as the current state in the next iteration. The algorithm specifies no computational-time bound.

Let $S$ be a nonempty finite set, let $A(s)$ be a nonempty finite set for each $s\in S$, and let $D=\{(s,a):s\in S,\ a\in A(s)\}$. Here **finite** means bijective with a natural number. Put $S_0=|S|$ and $A_0=\max_{s\in S}|A(s)|$. Fix a discount $0\le\gamma<1$. Give $S$ and $D$ their discrete sigma-algebras and give $[0,1]$ its Borel sigma-algebra. A **bounded-reward finite discounted Markov decision process** is a probability kernel $K$ from $D$ to $S\times[0,1]$. At pair $(s,a)$, $K(\cdot\mid s,a)$ is the joint law of the next state and the reward; these two coordinates need not be independent. Define the state-transition probabilities and expected rewards by

$$P(s'\mid s,a)=K(\{s'\}\times[0,1]\mid s,a),\qquad r(s,a)=\int_{S\times[0,1]}\rho\,K(ds',d\rho\mid s,a).$$

A **history-dependent behavior** is a sequence of probability kernels from observed-history spaces $H_t$ to the finite action alphabet $\mathcal A=\bigcup_{s\in S}A(s)$, assigning probability zero to actions outside $A(s_t)$ at every history ending in state $s_t$. Here $H_t$ consists of histories $(s_0,a_0,R_1,s_1,\ldots,a_{t-1},R_t,s_t)$, with discrete sigma-algebras on finite state/action coordinates and the Borel sigma-algebra on each reward coordinate; it has the resulting finite-product sigma-algebra. A **stationary Markov policy** assigns one distribution on $A(s)$ to each state, independently of earlier history. During interaction, after choosing $a_t$ in state $s_t$, the next pair $(s_{t+1},R_{t+1})$ is drawn from $K(\cdot\mid s_t,a_t)$.

Assume AC, fix a bounded-reward finite discounted MDP, an initial state, and a learning algorithm whose behavior is a history-dependent policy. At time $t\ge1$, let $h_t$ be the observed history ending at state $s_t$. The continuation behavior $A_t$ is the tail of the algorithm's action kernels after $h_t$, and $V^{A_t}(h_t)$ is the expected discounted return of the continuation process generated from that fixed history by those tail kernels. Set $S=|S|$ and $A=\max_{s\in S}|A(s)|$.
For $\epsilon\ge0$, the $\epsilon$-bad-step count is
$$N_\epsilon=\#\{t\ge1:V^{A_t}(h_t)<V^*(s_t)-\epsilon\},$$
where the count may be infinite. For $\epsilon>0$ and $0<\delta<1$, a PAC-MDP bound is a specified finite function $B(S,A,\epsilon,\delta,\gamma)$ such that, for every MDP with these finite state/action sizes and every initial state, $\mathbb P(N_\epsilon\le B(S,A,\epsilon,\delta,\gamma))\ge1-\delta$. This definition does not require the bad steps to precede a permanent stopping time.

For each fixed $t$, the finite-horizon continuation values are measurable functions of $h_t$: recursively, they are finite sums and integrals of nonnegative product-measurable functions against the behavior and MDP kernels. The kernel-integration theorem applies at each recursion, and the infinite-horizon value is the increasing limit of these finite-horizon values. Hence the bad-time sets and the extended count $N_\epsilon$ are measurable, so the displayed probability is defined.

derivations.claim: Initially both action values equal $0$, so the fixed tie order chooses $b$. Its next state is the same state and its reward is $0$. Before the $m$th observation it remains unknown at value $0$. Since $\gamma=0$ and $\beta=1/2$, the sweep count is $L=\max\{1,\lceil\ln 2\rceil\}=1$; on reaching $m$ samples, its empirical reward mean is $0$ and this sweep gives its known backup $0$, while the unvisited action $a$ still has heuristic value $0$.

The rebuilt values remain tied at zero, so the tie order again selects $b$. Induction over subsequent visits shows $a$ is never sampled and the table always has $Q(s,a)=Q(s,b)=0$. The heuristic is inadmissible since $U(a)=0<1=Q^*(s,a)$. At every time the continuation reward is zero, while $V^*(s)=1$, so $0<1-1/2$ and every time is bad.

In every bounded-reward finite discounted Markov decision process with nonempty finite state set $S$, nonempty finite action sets $A(s)$, and $0\le\gamma<1$, the trajectory law of every history-dependent behavior from every starting state exists. $$T^*V(s)=\max_{a\in A(s)}\left[r(s,a)+\gamma\sum_{s'\in S}P(s'\mid s,a)V(s')\right]$$

This fixed point is the supremum of the values of all history-dependent behaviors and is attained by a deterministic stationary greedy policy. The optimal action value is

$$Q^*(s,a)=r(s,a)+\gamma\sum_{s'\in S}P(s'\mid s,a)V^*(s'),$$

and $V^*(s)=\max_{a\in A(s)}Q^*(s,a)$ with $Q^*(s,a)\ge0$.

citations.quote: Let $S$ be a finite nonempty state set and let $A(s)$ be a finite nonempty action set for each $s\in S$, as in the finite-MDP convention. Put $D=\{(s,a):s\in S,\ a\in A(s)\}$ with its discrete sigma-algebra. Equip $S$ with its power-set sigma-algebra, $[0,1]$ with its Borel sigma-algebra, and $S\times[0,1]$ with the product sigma-algebra. A finite MDP with bounded real rewards specifies a probability kernel $Q$ from $D$ to $S\times[0,1]$; equivalently, each admissible $(s,a)$ has a probability measure $Q(\cdot\mid s,a)$ on that product measurable space. The reward-coordinate projection $(s',\rho)\mapsto\rho$ is measurable because the preimage of each Borel set $B\subseteq[0,1]$ is the product rectangle $S\times B$. Define the next-state law by $P(s'\mid s,a)=Q(\{s'\}\times[0,1]\mid s,a)$ and the mean reward by $r(s,a)=\int_{S\times[0,1]}\rho\,Q(ds',d\rho\mid s,a)\in[0,1]$. At each time, conditional on the observed history and the selected action, the next-state/reward pair has this law. Assume the Axiom of Choice for the path-space construction under policies.

Assume the Axiom of Choice for the path-law and conditional-expectation constructions. For a finite communicating MDP with rewards in $[0,1]$, let $V_n(s)$ be the supremum of the expected sum of the first $n$ rewards over all history-dependent policies starting from state $s$. For every state $s$, the limit $\lim_{n\to\infty}V_n(s)/n$ exists, is independent of $s$, and belongs to $[0,1]$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice for the path laws and conditional-expectation constructions used by the common-average-reward result. For a finite communicating MDP, let $\rho^*$ denote the common optimal average reward. The existence and independence of this value from the initial state are proved in the immediately cited theorem. Under any policy, write $R_T=\sum_{t=1}^T\rho_t$ for the realized cumulative reward over the first $T$ interactions. The pathwise regret is the random variable $\Delta_T=T\rho^*-R_T$. Its expected regret is $\mathbb E[\Delta_T]=T\rho^*-\mathbb E[R_T]$. The pathwise random variable and its expectation are distinct objects.

Assume the Axiom of Choice for the policy path laws used in the expectations below. For a finite MDP with bounded rewards, a policy assigns a probability distribution on $A(s)$ to each finite observed history ending in state $s$, with each action probability a measurable function of the history; deterministic policies are included. For states $x,y$, start at $S_0=x$ and define $\tau_y=\inf\{t\ge0:S_t=y\}$, with $\tau_y=+\infty$ if $y$ is never hit. This is an extended nonnegative measurable random variable because $\{\tau_y\le n\}=\bigcup_{t=0}^n\{S_t=y\}$. Take the expectation and the infimum over policies in $[0,+\infty]$. The MDP is communicating if $\inf_\pi\mathbb E_x^\pi[\tau_y]<\infty$ for every ordered pair $(x,y)$. Its raw diameter is $D_0=\sup_{x,y}\inf_\pi\mathbb E_x^\pi[\tau_y]$ in $[0,+\infty]$, and its normalized diameter is $D=\max\{1,D_0\}$ in the extended order. Since $S$ is finite, $D_0$ is finite for every communicating MDP. Thus a one-state MDP has $D_0=0$ and $D=1$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: The only state reaches itself at time $0$, so [F4] says the MDP is communicating. The unique action has expected reward $1/2$ at each time, so its finite-horizon value is $V_n=n/2$. By [F2], $\rho^*=\lim_nV_n/n=1/2$.
